subject: geography

moments.title: Soho outbreak
moments.who: Around 600 deaths in the Broad Street area
moments.body: A cholera outbreak hits Soho, London. Within 10 days, more than 500 people die in the streets around Broad Street. The dominant theory of disease is 'miasma' — bad air.
moments.takeaway: Mid-Victorian London regularly suffered cholera outbreaks. The disease's cause was contested between miasma theory and emerging germ theory.

moments.title: The pump handle
moments.body: Snow maps deaths around Broad Street and identifies the public water pump as the source. He persuades the Board of Guardians of St James's, Westminster, to remove the pump handle. New cases fall sharply.

quote.text: I had an interview with the Board of Guardians of St James's parish, on the evening of Thursday the 7th September, and represented the above circumstances to them. In consequence of what I said, the handle of the pump was removed on the following day.
quote.attrib: John Snow, 'On the Mode of Communication of Cholera', 1855

moments.takeaway: The map and the action are jointly the foundation of disease geography. Snow had been arguing since 1849 that cholera was waterborne.

moments.title: Great Stink and Bazalgette
moments.body: Hot summer 1858: the Thames stinks so badly that Parliament debates abandoning Westminster. Disraeli's government passes legislation enabling the Metropolitan Board of Works to build London's sewer system. Bazalgette's network (1859-1875) carries waste downstream of London; cholera does not return in epidemic form.
moments.takeaway: Public health infrastructure followed political incentive (smell at Westminster) more than scientific consensus (germ theory was not generally accepted until the 1860s).

now.title: Maps that change policy
now.body: Snow's map is one of the most reproduced in geography. The discipline of medical geography traces back to it. COVID-19 mapping (Johns Hopkins, ONS) revived public attention on disease geography. Cholera still kills tens of thousands worldwide each year, mainly in conflict zones (Yemen 2016-onwards, DRC).
now.open_questions: How much did Snow's map actually persuade contemporaries? Some historians argue the outbreak was already declining; others that the case was made gradually over years.

reflection: A single map showing what people already knew — clustered deaths around a water source — could push political action that medical theory could not. Visualisation is itself an act of geographical argument.
